props.title: The Crazies
props.initialSlug: Military virus turns small town into violent chaos

sections.content: George Romero's The Crazies (1973) pioneered viral outbreak horror before it became a mainstream subgenre. Unlike his zombie masterpiece Night of the Living Dead (1968), The Crazies presents a more grounded terror - a military-made toxin turning ordinary citizens violent. The film's influence echoes through modern outbreak films like 28 Days Later (2002) and Contagion (2011), establishing core genre elements: hazmat suits, military quarantines, and the breakdown of social order.

sections.content: Romero's signature social commentary shines through The Crazies' low-budget execution. The film brutally critiques military overreach and government incompetence - themes that would later define classics like RoboCop (1987) and They Live (1988). The chaos of local authorities arguing with military officials while citizens die creates a disturbing parallel to real-world crisis responses.

The film's visual style - documentary-like footage mixed with chaotic action sequences - influenced found footage horror like [REC] (2007) and Quarantine (2008). The clinical hazmat imagery contrasted with violent outbursts became a template for modern infection films like World War Z (2013). SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Pandemic Horror

sections.content: Modern filmmakers continue drawing from The Crazies' playbook. The 2010 remake starring Timothy Olyphant updated the original's themes for post-9/11 audiences, while films like Train to Busan (2016) and The Girl with All the Gifts (2016) merge viral outbreak tropes with zombie elements. Even serious pandemic dramas like 93 Days (2016) about the Ebola crisis echo Romero's focus on institutional failure.
